stimuli.text: Initial-rate data for A + B → products:
A student heats 11.8 g of $$\ce{CaCO3(s)}$$, which decomposes completely: $$\ce{CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g)}$$. The $$\ce{CO2}$$ is collected at 306 K and 1.03 atm.
The decomposition of compound X was monitored at constant temperature.
A student titrates 40.0 mL of 0.12 M weak monoprotic acid HA (Ka = 3 \times 10^{-5}) with 0.13 M NaOH.
3.9 g of $$\ce{NaOH}$$ dissolves in 135 g of water in a coffee-cup calorimeter. The temperature rises by 3 °C. Assume the solution's specific heat is 4.18 J/(g·°C).

A galvanic cell is made of a Zn electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Zn^{2+}}$$ and a Pb electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Pb^{2+}}$$. Standard reduction potentials: $$\ce{Zn^{2+} + 2e- -> Zn}$$ E° = -0.76 V; $$\ce{Pb^{2+} + 2e- -> Pb}$$ E° = -0.13 V.
The photoelectron spectra of Mg (Z = 12) and Al (Z = 13) are compared.

questions.stem: How many moles are in 200 g of $$\ce{H2SO4}$$?

options.why: Correct. n = m/M with M = 98.09 g/mol.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.01 M solution of $$\ce{NaOH}$$ at 25 °C?

options.why: Strong acids and bases ionize completely; no equilibrium is needed.
Correct. Strong base: [OH⁻] = 1 × 0.01 M; pH = 14 − pOH.
That is the pOH; subtract from 14.

questions.stem: How many moles of gas are in a 36 L flask at 0.202 atm and 286 K?
Adding an inert gas to a reaction mixture at constant volume does what to the equilibrium?

options.text: Shifts it toward more gas moles
Nothing; partial pressures of the reacting gases are unchanged
Shifts it toward fewer gas moles

questions.stem: Why is HI a stronger acid than HF?

options.text: F is less electronegative than I
The H–I bond is weaker and I⁻ is larger, so H⁺ is released more easily
options.why: Correct. Bond strength decreases down the group.

questions.explanation: Bond strength decreases down the group.

questions.stem: 19 mL of 11.5 M solution is diluted to 262 mL. What is the new concentration?

options.why: V₂ is the total final volume.

questions.stem: Which bond is the most polar?

options.why: Correct. It has the largest electronegativity difference (1.8).

questions.stem: On a reaction energy profile, the reactants are at 70 kJ/mol, the transition state at 156 kJ/mol and the products at 15 kJ/mol. What is ΔH for the reaction?

options.why: Measure from the correct starting point.

questions.explanation: Forward Ea = 86, ΔH = -55, reverse Ea = 141 kJ/mol.

questions.stem: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 37 g. The actual yield is 30.7 g. What is the percent yield?
Which is the ground-state electron configuration of iron (Fe, Z = 26)?

options.why: Correct. Fill orbitals in order until 26 electrons are placed.

questions.stem: 57 g of water at 52 °C is mixed with 27 g of water at 13 °C in an insulated container. What is the final temperature?

options.why: Correct. Heat lost = heat gained; for water alone, a mass-weighted average.
Pair each mass with its own temperature.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{A(g) + B(g) <=> 2C(g)}$$, K = 1.7. A mixture has [A] = 0.5 M, [B] = 0.7 M and [C] = 0.5 M. In which direction will the reaction proceed?

options.text: It proceeds in reverse, toward reactants, because Q = 0.714
options.why: If Q is less than K, the reaction proceeds forward.

options.text: It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 1.43
It is at equilibrium, because Q = K
It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 0.714
options.why: Correct. Q = [C]²/([A][B]) = 0.714, which is less than K.

questions.stem: Samples of $$\ce{He}$$, $$\ce{H2}$$, $$\ce{Cl2}$$, $$\ce{N2}$$ are all at the same temperature. Which has the highest average molecular speed?

options.why: Cl2 has a larger molar mass (70.9 g/mol).
N2 has a larger molar mass (28 g/mol).
Correct. At the same temperature, average kinetic energy is equal, so the lightest gas moves fastest.
He has a larger molar mass (4 g/mol).

questions.explanation: Molar masses: He 4, H2 2.02, Cl2 70.9, N2 28.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{4NH3 + 5O2 -> 4NO + 6H2O}$$, $$\ce{O2}$$ is consumed at 0.24 M/s. At what rate does $$\ce{H2O}$$ form?

options.why: Divide by the reactant's coefficient too.
Correct. Multiply by the coefficient ratio 6/5.

questions.stem: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH negative, which change shifts the equilibrium toward NH₃?

options.why: The reaction is exothermic; heating shifts left.
Correct. The product side has fewer moles of gas.

questions.explanation: The product side has fewer moles of gas.

questions.stem: A solution has an absorbance of 0.165 in a 2 cm cuvette. The molar absorptivity is 827 M⁻¹cm⁻¹. What is the concentration?
A reaction has K = 34. What is K for the reaction reversed and multiplied by 2?

options.why: K is raised to a power, not multiplied.
Multiplying by n raises K to the nth power.
Correct. Reverse → 1/K; multiply by n → Kⁿ.

questions.stem: Which substance has the highest boiling point?

options.why: Correct. Water forms extensive hydrogen bonds.

questions.stem: What is the pressure of 2 mol of gas in a 7 L container at 427 K?

options.why: With L and atm, use R = 0.08206.

questions.stem: 33 mL of 4.8 M solution is diluted to 339 mL. What is the new concentration?

options.why: V₂ is the total final volume.

questions.stem: A 33.7 mL sample of $$\ce{H2SO4}$$ is titrated to the equivalence point with 32.8 mL of 0.13 M NaOH. What is the concentration of the acid?

options.why: Correct. Each H₂SO₄ reacts with two OH⁻, so divide the moles of NaOH by 2.

questions.stem: Why does increasing temperature increase reaction rate?

options.text: A larger fraction of collisions have energy at or above the activation energy

questions.stem: How many moles of gas are in a 27 L flask at 3.21 atm and 434 K?
Why is the enthalpy of vaporization of water much larger than its enthalpy of fusion?

options.text: Vaporization separates molecules completely, overcoming all intermolecular forces

questions.stem: Which compound has the greater lattice energy, $$\ce{NaCl}$$ or $$\ce{CaO}$$?

options.text: They are equal because both are ionic
$$\ce{NaCl}$$, because it has more atoms per formula unit
options.why: Number of atoms does not determine lattice energy.

options.text: $$\ce{CaO}$$, because its ions have larger charges
options.why: Correct. By Coulomb's law, attraction increases with the product of the ion charges.

options.text: $$\ce{NaCl}$$, because its ions have larger charges

questions.explanation: CaO has ion charges 2 and 2; NaCl has 1 and 1.

questions.stem: A weak acid HA has pKa = 8.7. In a solution at pH 9.2, which statement is correct?

options.why: Correct. Above the pKa, the deprotonated form dominates.

questions.stem: What is the mass percent of C in $$\ce{C6H12O6}$$?

options.why: Use masses, not numbers of atoms.
That is the percent of the other elements.
There are 6 atoms of C in the formula.

questions.stem: How many valence electrons are shown in the Lewis structure of $$\ce{O3}$$?

options.why: Correct. Sum the valence electrons of all atoms, then add one per negative charge (subtract one per positive charge).

questions.stem: A mass spectrum of a sample of lithium shows two peaks: mass 6 with relative abundance 71% and mass 7 with 29%. What is the average atomic mass of the sample?

options.why: Pair each mass with its own abundance.
The isotopes are not equally abundant.
Correct. Weight each isotope mass by its fractional abundance.

questions.stem: A gas mixture contains 0.4 mol N₂, 0.6 mol O₂ and 0.9 mol Ar at a total pressure of 3.1 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: The gases are not present in equal amounts.
Use the mole fraction, not moles.

questions.stem: Calculate ΔH° for $$\ce{C2H5OH + 3O2 -> 2CO2 + 3H2O(l)}$$. (ΔH°f of O₂ is 0.)

options.why: Correct. Σ n ΔH°f(products) − Σ n ΔH°f(reactants).
Multiply each ΔH°f by its coefficient.

questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of S in $$\ce{SO2}$$?

options.why: Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Correct. The oxidation numbers must sum to the species' overall charge (O usually −2, H usually +1).
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.

questions.stem: A first-order reaction has a half-life of 9 min. Starting at 12 M, what is the concentration after 36 min?

options.why: Each half-life halves the concentration; it is not divided by 2n.

questions.stem: How should acetic acid be written in a net ionic equation?

options.why: Correct. It is a weak acid and mostly un-ionized.

options.text: It is always omitted as a spectator

questions.explanation: It is a weak acid and mostly un-ionized.

questions.stem: Steel is harder than pure iron because:

options.text: Small carbon atoms in the gaps (interstitial alloy) hinder layers of iron atoms from sliding
Carbon replaces iron atoms of the same size

questions.stem: What is the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 0.109 mol of solute in enough water to make 310 mL of solution?
What is the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 0.088 mol of solute in enough water to make 393 mL of solution?
In a Zn/Cu galvanic cell, [Zn²⁺] is increased. What happens to the cell potential?

options.why: Correct. A product's concentration rises, so Q increases.

questions.explanation: A product's concentration rises, so Q increases.

questions.stem: The Ksp of $$\ce{PbI2}$$ is 7.1 \times 10^{-9}. What is its molar solubility in pure water?
A weak acid HA has pKa = 4. In a solution at pH 6.5, which statement is correct?

options.why: Correct. Above the pKa, the deprotonated form dominates.

questions.stem: A weak acid (pKa 3.75) is titrated with NaOH; the equivalence point is reached at 26.6 mL. What is the pH after 13.3 mL of NaOH has been added?

options.why: That is only for strong acid–strong base equivalence.
Correct. At the half-equivalence point, [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa.

questions.stem: Is $$\ce{SiH4}$$ polar or nonpolar, and why?

options.text: Nonpolar, because its bond dipoles cancel by symmetry
Polar, because its bond dipoles do not cancel
options.why: Consider the molecule's shape, not only its bonds.
Containing H does not make a molecule polar.

options.text: Polar, because all its bonds are polar
options.why: Polarity depends on both bond polarity and geometry.

questions.explanation: SiH4 is tetrahedral; the dipoles cancel.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g)}$$, initial [H₂] = 1 M and [I₂] = 0.6 M, with no HI. At equilibrium, [HI] = 0.28 M. What is K?
For $$\ce{2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O}$$, 41 g of $$\ce{H2}$$ reacts with 29 g of $$\ce{O2}$$. What mass of $$\ce{H2O}$$ can form?

options.why: Apply the mole ratio from the equation.
Use the limiting reactant, which gives less product.
Correct. O2 is the limiting reactant.
Not all of both reactants reacts.

questions.stem: The first four ionization energies of an element are 742, 1350, 8100, 15309 kJ/mol. In which group of the periodic table is the element most likely found?

options.why: Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.
Correct. The large jump comes after removing 2 electrons, so it has 2 valence electrons.
Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.
Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.

questions.explanation: The big jump marks the start of removing core electrons.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{2Na + Cl2 -> 2NaCl}$$, 69 g of $$\ce{Na}$$ reacts with 52 g of $$\ce{Cl2}$$. What mass of $$\ce{NaCl}$$ can form?

options.why: Apply the mole ratio from the equation.
Use the limiting reactant, which gives less product.
Not all of both reactants reacts.
Correct. Cl2 is the limiting reactant.

questions.explanation: Na: 3 mol → 3 mol NaCl; Cl2: 0.733 mol → 1.47 mol. 1.47 mol × 58.44 = 85.7 g.

questions.stem: At 298 K, ΔG° for a reaction is -17 kJ/mol. What is K?

options.why: Correct. K = e^(−ΔG°/RT), with ΔG° in J/mol and R = 8.314.

questions.explanation: ln K = 6.86; K = 955. Negative ΔG°: K greater than 1.

questions.stem: Use the bond enthalpies to estimate ΔH for $$\ce{H2 + Br2 -> 2HBr}$$.

options.why: Correct. ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed).
Broken minus formed, not formed minus broken.
Bonds formed release energy: subtract them.
Multiply each bond energy by the number of bonds.

questions.stem: What is the energy of a photon with a wavelength of 255 nm?

options.why: Correct. E = hc/λ, with λ in meters.

questions.stem: A photoelectron spectrum shows 3 peaks. From highest to lowest binding energy, their relative heights are 2 : 2 : 3. Which element is it?

options.why: Correct. The peaks correspond to $$1s^{2}\,2s^{2}\,2p^{3}$$, which has 7 electrons.

questions.stem: A first-order reaction has a rate constant of 0.0533 min⁻¹. What is its half-life?
A reaction has ΔH° = -38 kJ/mol and ΔS° = -226 J/(mol·K). Below what temperature is it thermodynamically favorable?

options.why: Correct. Set ΔG = 0: T = ΔH/ΔS (with ΔH in J).
Convert ΔH to J (or ΔS to kJ).

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.5 M solution of formic acid (Ka = 1.8 \times 10^{-4})?

options.why: A weak acid does not ionize completely.
Correct. Solve Ka = x²/(C − x) for x = [H₃O⁺].

questions.stem: What is the rate law?

options.why: Recheck how the rate changes when [B] doubles.
Orders are found from the data, not from coefficients.
Compare trials where only one concentration changes.
Correct. Doubling [A] multiplies the rate by 4; doubling [B] multiplies it by 1.

questions.explanation: Trials 1→2: rate ×4, so order 2 in A. Trials 1→3: rate ×1, so order 0 in B.

questions.stem: Reaction 1 has ΔH₁ = -401 kJ and reaction 2 has ΔH₂ = 25 kJ. A target reaction is obtained by doubling reaction 1 and adding reaction 2. What is ΔH for the target reaction?

options.why: Correct. Reverse → change sign; multiply → multiply ΔH; then add.
Reversing changes the sign of ΔH₂.
Enthalpies add; they do not multiply.

questions.stem: When a reaction involving 0.033 mol of limiting reactant occurs in 126 g of solution (c = 4.18 J/(g·°C)), the temperature falls by 14.7 °C. What is ΔH for the reaction?

options.why: Correct. q(solution) = mcΔT = 7740 J; q(reaction) = −q(solution); divide by moles.
A temperature rise means the reaction is exothermic (negative ΔH).
Divide by the moles of reactant.

questions.stem: A reaction has ΔH° = -172 kJ/mol and ΔS° = -124 J/(mol·K). Below what temperature is it thermodynamically favorable?

options.why: Convert ΔH to J (or ΔS to kJ).
Correct. Set ΔG = 0: T = ΔH/ΔS (with ΔH in J).

questions.stem: A buffer contains 0.2 mol of a weak acid HA (pKa 9.25) and 0.38 mol of its conjugate base A⁻. Then 0.05 mol of HCl is added. What is the pH?

options.why: Correct. First react: H⁺ converts A⁻ to HA. Then pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]).
Update moles after the added acid or base reacts.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.2 M solution of hydrofluoric acid (Ka = 6.8 \times 10^{-4})?

options.why: A weak acid does not ionize completely.
Correct. Solve Ka = x²/(C − x) for x = [H₃O⁺].

questions.stem: What is E°cell for a galvanic cell made from these half-cells?

options.why: Cathode minus anode; a galvanic cell is positive.
E° does not change when half-reactions are multiplied.

parts.prompt: Calculate the number of moles of CO₂ produced.

rubric.criterion: Correct moles using molar mass 100.09 g/mol and the 1:1 ratio.

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of CO₂ expected.
The student measures 2.558 L of gas. Calculate the percent yield, and give one experimental reason the yield could be less than 100%.

rubric.example: Incomplete decomposition (not heated long enough) or gas leaking from the apparatus.

parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a complete Lewis diagram for CO₂, and identify its molecular geometry and the hybridization of carbon.

rubric.example: O=C=O with two lone pairs on each O (16 valence electrons).

parts.prompt: Explain why CO₂ is nonpolar even though C=O bonds are polar.

rubric.criterion: Linear symmetry makes the bond dipoles cancel.

parts.prompt: CaO is an ionic solid. Explain, using Coulomb's law, why CaO has a higher melting point than KCl.

rubric.criterion: Larger ion charges in CaO (2+/2−) than in KCl (1+/1−).
Greater electrostatic attraction (and smaller ions) means more energy is needed to separate the ions.

parts.prompt: Calculate the average rate of disappearance of X between 0 and 20 s.
Determine the order of the reaction with respect to X. Justify your answer using the data.

rubric.example: Equal time intervals give equal changes in 1/[X].

parts.prompt: Write the rate law and determine the rate constant, with units.
Calculate the half-life of the reaction (for the initial concentration).
A proposed mechanism has a slow first step: 2X → X₂. Is the mechanism consistent with the rate law? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Yes; the slow step's elementary rate law matches the observed rate law.

parts.prompt: A catalyst is added. Explain its effect on the rate and on the rate constant, using activation energy.

rubric.example: The catalyst provides a new pathway.

rubric.criterion: Lower activation energy means a larger fraction of collisions are successful.

parts.prompt: Write the net ionic equation for the titration reaction.
Calculate the initial pH of the acid solution.

rubric.criterion: Ka expression set up with x = [H₃O⁺].

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of NaOH needed to reach the equivalence point.
What is the pH at the half-equivalence point? Justify.
Calculate the pH at the equivalence point.

rubric.criterion: Uses Kb = Kw/Ka and the diluted [A⁻].

parts.prompt: Choose an appropriate indicator from: methyl orange (pKa 3.7), bromothymol blue (pKa 7.0), phenolphthalein (pKa 9.3). Justify.

rubric.criterion: Indicator whose pKa is closest to the equivalence pH.

parts.prompt: Explain why the solution at the half-equivalence point resists pH change when a small amount of HCl is added.

rubric.criterion: A⁻ reacts with added H⁺ to form HA (buffer).
rubric.example: A⁻ + H₃O⁺ → HA + H₂O, so the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] changes only slightly.

parts.prompt: Is the dissolution endothermic or exothermic? Justify.

rubric.example: Exothermic: the solution warmed, so energy was released.

parts.prompt: Calculate the heat absorbed or released by the solution.
Calculate ΔH of dissolution in kJ/mol.
If some heat escaped to the surroundings, would the magnitude of the calculated ΔH be too large or too small? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Too small, because the measured temperature change is smaller than the true change.

parts.prompt: Write the balanced net ionic equation for the cell reaction.
Calculate E°cell.
Calculate ΔG° for the cell reaction.
The concentration of Zn²⁺ is increased to 2.0 M. Predict the effect on the cell potential and justify.

rubric.criterion: E decreases because Q increases (a product's concentration rises).
rubric.example: Q greater than 1 → E less than E°.

questions.title: Solubility of a slightly soluble salt

parts.prompt: Write the Ksp expression.
Calculate the molar solubility in pure water.
Calculate the molar solubility in a solution containing 0.01 M I⁻ (from a soluble salt).
Would lowering the pH significantly change the solubility? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Correct reasoning about whether the anion is basic.
rubric.example: No: I⁻ is the conjugate base of a strong acid, so H⁺ does not remove it.

parts.prompt: Write the electron configuration of Al.
Explain why the 1s peak of Al has a higher binding energy than the 1s peak of Mg.

rubric.criterion: Al has more protons, so 1s electrons are attracted more strongly (Coulomb's law).

parts.prompt: Describe one difference in the number or relative height of peaks between the two spectra.

rubric.criterion: A valid difference based on configurations.
rubric.example: Al has one more electron, so its outermost peak is taller or an extra peak appears.

parts.prompt: Which element has the larger atomic radius? Justify using Coulomb's law.

rubric.criterion: Mg: fewer protons with similar shielding, so valence electrons are held less tightly.
rubric.example: Same period; effective nuclear charge increases across.
